title: Savaiye close
hookLine: the ten verses sharpen one point: love, not display

lines: THE GURU WHO GAVE THE KHALSA ITS FORM.
WROTE THAT FORM WITHOUT LOVE IS NOTHING.
cards: Here's a strange thing about the man who wrote the ten savaiye.
Guru Gobind Singh gave the Khalsa its outward form: the five articles Sikhs who take amrit keep on their bodies every day, uncut hair, a comb, a steel bracelet, cotton undershorts, the kirpan.
He shaped how a whole community looks, to this day. And the same Guru wrote ten verses saying outward forms, without love, aren't worth a single seed. Is that a contradiction?

teach.h: TEN VERSES, ONE MOVE: WEIGH IT.
teach.b: First, lay the ten verses side by side. They make the same move every time: set up something impressive, then weigh it. Tav prasad over the door: cupped hands, waiting.
The ascetics of every order: not one ratti without love. Maate matang: their kings left barefoot. The conquerors: the drums faded.
The crane with its eyes shut: still, and hunting. Bhed, with compassion and charity on the list: the secret missed. Then the line the set leans on: those who loved, they alone found the Lord.
Ten verses, one point, sharpened until it cuts.
Love, not display. Now the question from the hook. Sikhs don't hear the savaiye as saying the outward form doesn't matter.

teach.h: SAID AS THE AMRIT IS PREPARED.
teach.b: The same verses are recited while the amrit is prepared, at the very ceremony where people take on the five articles. So the form and the warning are given in the same breath, on purpose.

teach.h: THE FORM IS A CUP FOR THE LOVE.
teach.b: As some Sikh teachers put it, the form is meant to carry the love, the way a cup carries water. A beautiful cup that's empty is still empty, but nobody throws it away for that.

They fill it. The danger the savaiye name is the cup admired for itself: the turban worn for show, the bani rushed to be done, the kirpan as a costume. And the savaiye let no one off: not kings, not yogis, not pilgrims.
Many readers hear the warning reaching the Khalsa too, since these verses are said at its own initiation.

how: Many Sikhs recite all ten Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning after Jaap Sahib; they are also read while amrit is prepared at the Khalsa initiation, where initiates take on the five articles of faith.

o: the five articles every Khalsa Sikh keeps
short hymns sung at the close of the day
four-line verses; here, ten said each morning

games.why: the savaiye are recited as the amrit is prepared, form and warning given together. many Sikhs say the form carries the love, and the danger is the cup admired for itself.

practice: Think back over the week's verses, the ascetics, the elephants, the conquerors, the crane, the rituals, the line about love, and notice which one stayed with you.
If you have the text or a recording, read or hear that savaiya again, slowly; if not, replay its picture in your mind. Ask what caught you, and if you pray, say Waheguru when you've finished.

wordCard.voice: Savaiye, four-line verses. Ten of them weigh the ascetics, the elephants, the conquerors, the crane and every ritual, and find only love was ever heavy enough.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: savaiye, the plural of savaiya, the four-line verse form of these ten.
